newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Rating agency wrong about change of NZ govt-Bolger.
newsitem.headline: Rating agency wrong about change of NZ govt-Bolger.

text.p: Prime Minister Jim Bolger said international credit rating agencies have got it wrong when they said a change of government would not affect New Zealand's sovereign rating.
Standard & Poor's said on Wednesday that it did not regard the election due on October 12 as a threat to New Zealand's AA+ credit rating.
Bolger told a business gathering in Auckland that S&P got it wrong in 1990 when it was planning a double downgrade of New Zealand even though a conservative National government was elected.

Both S&P and Moody's Investors Service have consistently said for some time that even if there was a change of government they did not expect any major policy shift that would undermine New Zealand's economic framework.
S&P Sovereign Risk Managing Director David Beers told an audience in New York on Wednesday that the New Zealand economy was the strongest it had been in years.
He said there could be a slowdown after the election but a new government was unlikely to depart drastically from current policies.
"We actually think that there's a cushion there in economic and financial terms which will allow the new government time to figure out how to operate under the new rules," he said.
S&P upgraded New Zealand's foreign currency rating in January to AA+ from AA, citing government debt reduction as its main reason.
